perspective:
Mason’s available information:

- He is an accountant at a small community center and knows Martha Moua as a personal care aide colleague there; their relationship is professional and work-focused.
- While reviewing the community center’s financial reports, Mason observed discrepancies: healthcare expenses looked unusually high and did not match usual spending patterns. This led him to suspect Martha might be mismanaging funds, and he felt suspicious and anxious.
- He asked Martha to discuss the recent financial report and told her some numbers did not add up. He heard Martha say there was likely a reasonable explanation and ask which discrepancies he meant.
- Mason pointed to the unusually high healthcare expenses. He heard Martha say it might have been a misentry and that she would review and correct any errors.
- After reviewing the matter with Martha, Mason concluded the discrepancies were due to a simple clerical error, not mismanagement. He felt relieved and embarrassed about his initial suspicion.
- He told Martha he appreciated her quick clarification and said it seemed to be just a clerical error. He heard Martha say errors happen and she was glad they cleared it up. Mason apologized for his initial suspicion and said he should have asked her first. Martha said it was okay, understood he was being thorough, and suggested double-checking entries next time.
- Mason now believes Martha is competent, but he thinks the recurring clerical errors show that the financial management system is inadequate. He feels frustrated with the system and empathetic toward Martha.
- He told Martha the issue was not her management but the current system. He proposed drafting a new, more robust financial system and asked for her input. Martha agreed and offered to help address the gaps they identified.
- Mason drafted the proposal. He hoped it would benefit operations but was uncertain whether management would approve and implement it. He told Martha he had finished the draft and was unsure how management would receive it. Martha encouraged him to present confidently and said the benefits were clear. Mason asked her to help gather data, and she agreed.
- Mason presented the proposal to management and believed the presentation went well. He felt satisfied but physically and mentally exhausted, and believed he had done everything possible. He told Martha it was now up to management. Martha praised his work and suggested he take time off. Mason planned to take a few days off to recharge and reflect, hoping for good news. Martha wished him a good break and offered help while he was away.

He does not have access to management’s final decision or Martha’s private thoughts beyond what she said aloud.
